papers.title: Constraining the Inner Dark Matter Profiles of Strong-Lensing Galaxy Clusters
papers.authors: Emma M. Strickland, Zelie Goldberg Little, Jackson H. O'Donnell, Tesla E. Jeltema
papers.abstract: We present mass modeling of three strong lensing galaxy clusters found in the Dark Energy Survey utilizing Hubble Space Telescope imaging for lens modeling, and complementary constraints from Chandra X-ray observations. All three clusters are relaxed and have giant arc or ring lens structures ideal for constraints on the dark matter distribution. The strong lens modeling and X-ray temperatures yield consistent total cluster mass estimates. We find these clusters have best-fit X-ray temperatures of $2.7 - 6.2$ keV and total masses of M$_{200} = (1-6) \times 10^{14} M_{\odot}$. Our lens models parameterize dark matter distribution with a generalized Navarro-Frenk-White (GNFW) density profile. While the GNFW profile allows the inner dark matter slope to vary, we find in all cases that the inner slopes are consistent with the standard NFW density profile $\gamma^{DM} = 1$. The X-ray surface brightness distributions for all three clusters are generally symmetric with no significant substructure, supporting the conclusion that these are relaxed clusters. In addition, we find generally low values of the external shear magnitude with median values ranging $|\gamma^{ext}| = 0.04-0.09$ and consistent with zero for two of the clusters.

conclusions: The recovered inner dark matter slopes for the three clusters are $\gamma^{\mathrm{DM}} = 0.85^{+0.09}_{-0.08}$, $0.89^{+0.16}_{-0.17}$, and $1.05^{+0.18}_{-0.19}$, all statistically consistent with a standard NFW cusp ($\gamma^{\mathrm{DM}} = 1$) and showing no evidence for flat cores from self-interacting dark matter.

Strong lensing and Chandra X-ray temperatures ($T_X = 2.7 - 6.2\text{ keV}$) yield mutually consistent total cluster halo masses in the range $M_{200m} \approx (1 - 6) \times 10^{14}\, M_{\odot}$ with concentrations $c_{200m} \approx 8 - 10$.

The X-ray emission is symmetric and lacks substructure, while the lens models require minimal external shear ($|\gamma^{\mathrm{ext}}| = 0.04 - 0.09$, consistent with zero for two clusters), confirming these systems are dynamically relaxed and well-described by a single spherical halo plus galaxy components.
ai.summary: Collisionless cold dark matter (CDM) predicts that dark matter halos have 'cuspy' inner density profiles where density rises steeply toward the center ($\rho \propto r^{-1}$), whereas alternative models like self-interacting dark matter (SIDM) transfer heat inward to form flatter central 'cores'. Testing this in galaxy clusters requires disentangling the dark matter halo from the central brightest cluster galaxy (BCG) and avoiding unrelaxed, merging clusters whose complex substructure biases mass reconstructions. The authors model three strong-lensing galaxy clusters from the Dark Energy Survey ($z \approx 0.4 - 0.6$) that exhibit near-ring giant arcs in Hubble Space Telescope imaging, using `PyAutoLens` and nested sampling (`dynesty`) to fit a generalized Navarro-Frenk-White (GNFW) halo profile alongside separate BCG and member-galaxy mass components. They combine this with Chandra X-ray observations to verify that the hot intracluster gas is smooth and symmetric—confirming the clusters are dynamically relaxed—and to obtain independent temperature-based mass estimates, demonstrating that these cluster cores are fully consistent with standard collisionless CDM.

papers.title: Emission line stacking on cosmological scales: equivalence to two-point statistics and modelling of the observational effects
papers.authors: Zhaoting Chen, José Luis Bernal
papers.abstract: Emission line stacking measurement for cosmological line intensity mapping (LIM) contains not only the average emission line profile of the stacked sources, but usually also the clustering signal, due to the limited angular resolution of the observations. We provide an explicit derivation of the equivalence between the emission line stacking, the two-point cross-correlation function in configuration space and the power spectrum in Fourier space, similar to the case between the angular stacking signal for the kinematic Sunyaev-Zel'dovich effect and the angular power spectrum in harmonic space ( arXiv:2512.14625 , arXiv:2605.15947 ). Using the quadratic estimator formalism, we establish that the emission line stacking signal measurement is equivalent to a quadratic estimator for the cross-correlation function. The formalism allows for the explicit modelling of the stacked signal, including the clustering statistics as well as observational effects such as the galaxy selection function and the LIM survey footprint. In particular, using mock HI intensity mapping data, we show that we can accurately model the effects of foreground removal on the stacked signal. The correlation function estimator provides significant speed-up for the stacking measurement and enables modelling of the signal and its covariance for large LIM datasets with MeerKLASS and future SKAO.

conclusions: 3D emission line stacking around catalogued galaxies is mathematically identical to the configuration-space two-point cross-correlation function $\xi[L, \delta](\bm{s})$ (and the inverse Fourier transform of the cross-power spectrum $P(\bm{k})$) between the intensity map and the galaxy overdensity field, reducing to the average source emission profile only in the shot-noise limit.

All linear observational and data-processing operations—such as PCA foreground cleaning, beam smoothing, survey footprint masking, galaxy selection weights, and aperture tapering—can be absorbed directly into the window function and transfer function of a quadratic cross-power spectrum estimator.

Validated on lognormal mock $\text{H}\textsc{i}$ intensity mapping simulations (including thermal noise, beam smoothing, and foreground removal), the quadratic estimator's analytical predictions and covariances match direct 3D and 1D aperture-tapered stacking measurements well within $1\sigma$.

Replacing source-by-source cubelet stacking with Fourier-space cross-power spectrum estimation eliminates the need for expensive forward modelling and provides a major computational speed-up for cross-correlating upcoming high-density galaxy surveys (like DESI) with large LIM datasets (like MeerKLASS and SKAO).
ai.relevance_reason: Provides useful background on two-point clustering estimators and observational window functions in large-scale structure, though its focus on 21cm line intensity mapping stacking is outside core work on beyond-ΛCDM simulations, emulators, and inhomogeneous cosmology.
ai.summary: Line intensity mapping (LIM) measures the integrated emission of spectral lines—such as the 21 cm hyperfine transition of neutral hydrogen ($\text{H}\textsc{i}$)—across large cosmic volumes without resolving individual galaxies. To boost the signal-to-noise ratio, analysts often "stack" (co-add) 3D sub-volumes (cubelets) of the intensity map centered on known galaxy positions from an overlapping optical survey; however, because LIM telescopes have coarse angular resolution (arcminutes to degrees), this stacked signal blends the intrinsic emission of the target galaxies with large-scale clustering from neighboring structures. The authors prove mathematically that 3D emission line stacking is formally equivalent to a quadratic estimator for the two-point cross-correlation function in configuration space (or the inverse Fourier transform of the cross-power spectrum) between the intensity map and the galaxy overdensity field. Using this formalism, they incorporate linear observational effects—including beam smoothing, galaxy selection functions, survey masks, and principal component analysis (PCA) foreground cleaning—directly into the estimator's window and transfer functions, validating their analytical model against lognormal mock $\text{H}\textsc{i}$ simulations. This equivalence eliminates the need for expensive forward modelling of galaxy profiles and drastically speeds up both stacking measurements and covariance estimation for large upcoming datasets like MeerKLASS and the Square Kilometre Array Observatory (SKAO).

papers.title: FastPM: Fast Pretrained Model for Cosmological Simulation-Based Inference
papers.authors: Masaya Yamamoto, Adrian E. Bayer
papers.abstract: Modern cosmology increasingly relies on large ensembles of expensive simulations to model the non-linear Universe and extract information from upcoming surveys. However, generating high-fidelity simulations---whether gravity-only N-body or full hydrodynamical---requires substantial computational resources. In this work, we demonstrate that transfer learning from fast low-fidelity simulations can dramatically reduce the cost of training machine learning models, in particular for simulation-based inference (SBI). We train a Fast Pretrained Model (FastPM) on a set of Fast Particle-Mesh (FastPM) simulations to infer $\Omega_m$ and $\sigma_8$ from the power spectrum, and finetune on a smaller set of high-fidelity CAMELS N-body and hydrodynamical simulations. To reach a fixed posterior accuracy, the pretrained model requires only 5--15\% of the high-fidelity simulations compared to the number of simulations needed when training on CAMELS alone, reducing the total training simulation compute cost, including that of the pretraining simulations, by up to an order of magnitude in CPU hours. Remarkably, the gains persist for the total matter power spectrum of full hydrodynamical simulations: although FastPM contains no baryonic physics, pretraining on FastPM runs that together cost less than a single hydrodynamical simulation still reduces the total training simulation compute by a factor of $\sim$5. Moreover, pretraining on more accurate FastPM runs yields more accurate posteriors than training on CAMELS alone achieves with any number of simulations we consider. These results demonstrate that transfer learning from fast simulations is a simple and powerful route to high-fidelity SBI, and highlight the promise of simulation-based foundation models in cosmology.

conclusions: Pretraining on just 2,000 ultra-fast 20-step FastPM simulations (costing ~2,000 CPU hours total, less than a single CAMELS hydro run at 3,000 CPU hours) cuts the number of CAMELS simulations needed to reach a benchmark accuracy ($\mathrm{NLTP} = 1$) by 80–90%, reducing the total end-to-end simulation compute budget by $8.8\times$ (N-body), $6.8\times$ (hydro CDM), and $4.7\times$ (hydro total matter).

With larger pretraining sets ($10^4$ FastPM runs), the required number of high-fidelity CAMELS simulations drops to just 5–15% of the baseline trained from scratch, saving up to an order of magnitude ($\sim 10\times$) in total CPU hours.

Transfer learning succeeds even when bridging the physics gap to full hydrodynamics: although gravity-only FastPM lacks baryonic feedback (which suppresses small-scale power and is degenerate with $\sigma_8$), pretraining captures the underlying gravitational cosmological dependence and avoids negative transfer.

Pretraining on $10^4$ higher-accuracy (200-step) FastPM runs achieves a lower asymptotic loss ($\mathrm{NLTP} \approx 0.5$–$0.6$) than training on up to 700 CAMELS runs alone ($\mathrm{NLTP} \approx 0.7$), while maintaining well-calibrated posteriors (verified via TARP coverage tests) with as few as $\ge 50$ high-fidelity runs.
ai.relevance_reason: Directly demonstrates multi-fidelity transfer learning from approximate PM simulations (FastPM, closely analogous to COLA) to high-fidelity N-body/hydro simulations for non-linear power spectrum inference and SBI.
ai.summary: Simulation-based inference (SBI)—where neural networks learn posterior distributions directly from forward simulations without assuming a Gaussian likelihood—is a powerful way to extract non-linear cosmological information on small scales ($k \le 5\,h\,\mathrm{Mpc}^{-1}$), but training these networks normally requires thousands of computationally expensive N-body or hydrodynamical simulations. To overcome this bottleneck, the authors use transfer learning: they first pretrain a neural posterior estimator (a normalizing flow paired with an MLP embedding network) on thousands of cheap, approximate Fast Particle-Mesh (FastPM) gravity-only simulations to infer $\Omega_m$ and $\sigma_8$ from the matter power spectrum at $z=0$. They then fine-tune this pretrained network using a small fraction of expensive, high-fidelity N-body and IllustrisTNG hydrodynamical simulations from the CAMELS suite (which also marginalize over four stellar and AGN feedback parameters). This multi-fidelity strategy works remarkably well even when transferring from pure gravity to full hydrodynamics, slashing total computational costs by up to an order of magnitude while achieving tighter and better-calibrated posteriors than training on high-fidelity simulations alone.

papers.title: Halo formation and distribution around cosmic web
papers.authors: Hongfei Yu, Huiyuan Wang, Yangyao Chen, Ziwen Zhang, Hao Li
papers.abstract: We use the ELUCID simulation to study how the local environment affects the formation of dark matter halos and their spatial distribution around the cosmic web. We describe the environment by local density and cosmic-web type. At fixed web type, the halo mass function (HMF) depends strongly on the local density, whereas at fixed density it depends only weakly, though significantly, on the web type; the character of both dependencies changes around the mean density. The halo formation redshift is primarily driven by local density rather than cosmic web. We then introduce the three-dimensional cosmic-web cross-correlation function (3D-WCCF), which expresses the distribution of halos around cosmic web in the local tidal eigenframe. The 3D-WCCF provides numerous anisotropic characteristics. Around all web types, halos are most strongly correlated along the axis of weakest compression, $\mathbf{e}_3$, and least along the axis of strongest compression, $\mathbf{e}_1$. Nearly all cluster-sized halos reside in knots and lie preferentially in the plane perpendicular to ${\bf e}_1$. The 3D-WCCF also provides important information on the geometry and size of filaments, sheets and voids. Moreover, early-forming halos are more strongly correlated with the web than late-forming ones, and this assembly bias is anisotropic around filaments, sheets, and voids, being strongest along $\mathbf{e}_3$, but nearly isotropic around knots.

conclusions: **Density vs. cosmic-web type**: At fixed web type (smoothed at $R_{\rm s} = 2\,h^{-1}{\rm Mpc}$), the halo mass function (HMF) increases steeply with local density for $\delta < 0$ (rising by a factor of $\gtrsim 100$ as $\log(1+\delta)$ goes from $-0.5$ to $-0.1$) and flattens for $\delta > 0$ (changing by a factor of $< 2$). At fixed density, web-type dependence is weak but statistically significant, reversing across $\delta \sim 0$ (halos form most readily in voids for $\delta < 0$, and in knots for $\delta > 0$).

**Resolution of literature discrepancies**: Previous conflicting claims about whether local density or web type governs the HMF are explained by smoothing scale choices: web-type dependence at fixed $\delta$ nearly vanishes when smoothed at $R_{\rm s} = 10\,h^{-1}{\rm Mpc}$, and using mismatched smoothing scales for density and web classification artificially suppresses whichever quantity is smoothed on the larger scale.

**Halo formation time**: Mean halo formation redshift $\langle z_{\rm f} \rangle$ is driven almost entirely by local density rather than cosmic-web classification; at fixed $\delta$, differences in formation time across knots, filaments, sheets, and voids largely disappear.

**Anisotropic halo clustering (3D-WCCF)**: Across all web types and halo masses, halo cross-correlations obey $\xi_{\rm 3D}(r_3) \ge \xi_{\rm 3D}(r_2) \ge \xi_{\rm 3D}(r_1)$, showing that halos align with the axis of weakest tidal compression ($\mathbf{e}_3$). Characteristic structural scales emerge directly from the correlation sign changes and deficits, such as a filament width scale of $1.5\text{--}3.5\,h^{-1}{\rm Mpc}$ along $\mathbf{e}_1$ and a void radius of $\sim 13\,h^{-1}{\rm Mpc}$ along $\mathbf{e}_3$.

**Anisotropic assembly bias**: Early-forming low-mass halos cluster more strongly with the cosmic web than late-forming halos ($b_{\rm r} > 1$), and while this assembly bias is nearly isotropic around knots, it is strongly anisotropic around filaments, sheets, and voids—peaking along the $\mathbf{e}_3$ filament/extension axis.
ai.relevance_reason: While this is a standard $\Lambda$CDM simulation study, its quantification of how the tidal tensor eigenframe and smoothing scales affect halo abundance and assembly bias provides useful background for non-linear bias modelling ($s^2$ tidal bias in hybrid EFT) and smoothing-scale systematics in simulations.
ai.summary: Dark matter halos form and grow within the cosmic web—the large-scale network of knots, filaments, sheets, and voids shaped by gravitational tidal forces—but because cosmic-web classifications (based on the eigenvalues of the gravitational tidal tensor) strongly correlate with the local matter overdensity $\delta$, it has been debated which property actually drives halo abundance and assembly history. Using the dark-matter-only $\Lambda$CDM ELUCID $N$-body simulation ($500\,h^{-1}{\rm Mpc}$ box), the authors disentangle these effects by conditioning both the halo mass function (HMF) and halo formation redshift ($z_{\rm f}$, when a halo reaches half its final mass) jointly on local density and tidal web type at matched smoothing scales ($R_{\rm s} = 2\,h^{-1}{\rm Mpc}$), excluding "backsplash" halos (former satellites ejected from larger hosts). They further introduce a three-dimensional cosmic-web cross-correlation function (3D-WCCF) that measures halo clustering around web elements projected along the three local tidal eigenvectors—from strongest compression ($\mathbf{e}_1$) to weakest compression/extension ($\mathbf{e}_3$)—rather than averaging isotropically over angles. This matters because it resolves contradictions in past literature by tracing them to mismatched smoothing scales, while demonstrating that directional tidal structure governs both halo spatial distributions and secondary "assembly bias" (the dependence of halo clustering on age at fixed mass).

papers.title: Comment on "Test of the Gravitational Force Law on Cosmological Scales Using the Kinematic Sunyaev--Zeldovich Effect''
papers.authors: Alessandro Melchiorri
papers.abstract: Gallardo et al. [Phys. Rev. Lett. \textbf{136}, 151002 (2026)] constrain the index of the force law $g\propto r^{-n}$ with pairwise kinematic Sunyaev--Zeldovich measurements, $n=2.1\pm0.3$, and exclude the deep-MOND value $n=1$ at $3.3\sigma$. The exclusion does not follow from their calculation. Their templates for $n\neq2$ [their Eq.~(8)] raise the pair-averaged Newtonian acceleration to the power $n/2$, whereas the pair average of the pointwise law [their Eq.~(30) for deep MOND] is the average of the transformed field; the step that identifies the two attributes to the three-point function a correction that is of second order and not small. In a Gaussian linear field with linearly biased tracers, Gaussian integration by parts shows that the correctly averaged template is exactly proportional to the Newtonian one, with a constant that the analysis absorbs into the mean optical depth. Gaussian realizations with peak-selected tracers find the same proportionality to within 2\% (0.5\% for the fiducial selection), and refitting the data of the Letter with the resulting template gives $\chi^2=20.1$--$20.2$, against $20.1$ for the Newtonian template and $33.8$ for Eq.~(8): in every controlled case examined the data do not discriminate between $n=1$ and $n=2$, and the $3.3\sigma$ exclusion, with the $10\sigma$ forecast that rescales it, rests on the order in which the average and the power were taken. What a self-consistent MOND cosmology predicts for this observable is a separate question, which the Letter does not address.

conclusions: The previous claim by Gallardo et al. (2026) that pairwise kSZ measurements constrain the gravitational force law index to $n=2.1\pm 0.3$ and exclude deep MOND ($n=1$) at $3.3\sigma$ rests on taking the non-linear power after pair-averaging ($\langle g_N \rangle^{n/2}$) rather than averaging the pointwise force law ($\langle g_N^{n/2} \rangle$).

Using Stein's identity (Gaussian integration by parts), the author proves analytically that for a Gaussian linear density field with linearly biased tracers, the correctly averaged pairwise acceleration template for any force index $n > -2$ is strictly proportional to the Newtonian ($n=2$) radial profile, differing only by an overall constant $C_n \propto \frac{n+4}{6}\langle |\mathbf{g}|^{n/2-1}\rangle$.

In numerical Gaussian realizations with non-linear peak-selected tracers ($\nu > 1, 1.5, 2$), the ratio between the properly averaged deep-MOND ($n=1$) and Newtonian ($n=2$) pairwise profiles stays constant across $25\text{--}225\,\mathrm{Mpc}$ to within $0.5\text{--}2\%$ (compared to a factor of $3.3$ variation in the original paper's template).

Because the overall template amplitude is degenerate with the uncalibrated mean optical depth $\bar{\tau}$ of the galaxy clusters, refitting the ACT + BOSS data with the correctly averaged $n=1$ template yields $\chi^2 = 20.1\text{--}20.2$, identical to the Newtonian fit ($\chi^2 = 20.1$) and erasing the claimed $3.3\sigma$ exclusion ($\chi^2 = 33.8$) as well as the $10\sigma$ forecast for future surveys.
ai.relevance_reason: Directly addresses cosmological tests of modified gravity and highlights a crucial mathematical pitfall—that spatial/pair averaging does not commute with non-linear field transformations—which is closely related to both modified-gravity LSS modelling and averaging/backreaction in inhomogeneous cosmology.
ai.summary: The pairwise kinematic Sunyaev–Zeldovich (kSZ) effect—tiny temperature shifts in the CMB caused by cosmic microwave photons scattering off the hot gas in galaxy clusters moving toward each other—tracks the mean gravitational infall velocity of galaxy pairs and can test gravity on $30\text{--}230\,\mathrm{Mpc}$ scales. This comment refutes a recent *Physical Review Letters* paper by Gallardo et al. (2026) that claimed to rule out a deep-MOND gravitational force law ($g \propto r^{-1}$, as opposed to Newtonian $g \propto r^{-2}$) at $3.3\sigma$ using ACT CMB maps and SDSS BOSS galaxies. Melchiorri points out a fundamental mathematical error: because a non-linear function of an average is not the average of the function ($\langle g^{n/2}\rangle \neq \langle g\rangle^{n/2}$), raising the pair-averaged Newtonian acceleration template to the power $n/2$ fails to represent a pointwise modified force law, where a halo's total acceleration is dominated by its broader cosmic environment rather than a single distant partner. By analytically applying Gaussian integration by parts to a linear density field and verifying with numerical grid realizations of density peaks, the author shows that the properly pair-averaged $r^{-n}$ force template has the exact same radial shape as the Newtonian template, meaning the kSZ data cannot distinguish $n=1$ from $n=2$ once the unknown cluster optical depth amplitude is marginalized over.

papers.title: Correlations between Dynamical Dark Energy and Neutrino Parameters
papers.authors: Ching-Yu Leung, WangZheng Zhang, Ming-Chung Chu
papers.abstract: Recent Baryon Acoustic Oscillation (BAO) data from the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI), fitted jointly with Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) and Type Ia Supernovae (SNe) data, favor dynamical dark energy (DDE) over the standard $\Lambda$CDM model. In this work, we investigate whether the mass and degeneracy of relic neutrinos are degenerate with DDE parameters and can also account for this statistical deviation from $\Lambda$CDM. Using a Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) analysis of a joint Planck CMB temperature, DESI BAO, and Pantheon+ dataset, we show a robust parameter degeneracy between the DDE equation of state and neutrino physics. We supplement this with a semi-analytical framework that recovers the numerical correlation, showing that the tight constraint on the CMB acoustic scale drives this degeneracy. Our results highlight the clear correlation between DDE and neutrino parameters, underscoring the critical need to jointly constrain the neutrino sector and the dark sector in next-generation cosmological surveys.

conclusions: Fitting Planck CMB temperature, DESI BAO, and Pantheon+ SNe together under a standard $w_0w_a\text{CDM}$ model yields $(w_0, w_a) = (-0.769 \pm 0.079, -0.68^{+0.31}_{-0.27})$, representing $2.9\sigma$ and $2.2\sigma$ deviations from a cosmological constant.

When simultaneously varying neutrino parameters (applying Gaussian priors from previous CMB+lensing+BAO fits), the data accommodate a large total neutrino mass $M_\nu = 0.41 \pm 0.13\text{ eV}$, a third-eigenstate degeneracy parameter $\xi_{\nu_3} = 1.14^{+0.18}_{-0.13}$, and a higher Hubble constant $H_0 = 69.7 \pm 1.1\text{ km s}^{-1}\text{ Mpc}^{-1}$, while slightly shifting $(w_0, w_a)$ toward $(-0.796 \pm 0.079, -0.56^{+0.34}_{-0.30})$.

A semi-analytical Taylor expansion around fixed CMB acoustic scale $\theta_*$ and BAO angles closely reproduces the 2D MCMC posteriors, demonstrating that the tight constraint on $\theta_*$ is the primary driver of the correlation between $w_a$ and $\xi_{\nu_3}$ at fixed $M_\nu$ and $w_0$.

Because background geometric probes (CMB acoustic peaks, BAO, and SNe) cannot break the degeneracy between evolving dark energy and non-zero neutrino chemical potentials, precise measurements of large-scale structure growth will be required to distinguish between the two sectors.
ai.relevance_reason: Directly investigates parameter degeneracies in dynamical dark energy ($w_0w_a$) fits to Planck CMB, DESI BAO, and Pantheon+ SNe datasets, and highlights the necessity of non-linear structure growth measurements (like those from Euclid) to break background expansion degeneracies.

papers.title: Radio view of the Peanut cluster: merger-induced stripping and a radio halo shortly after pericentric passage
papers.authors: K. Rajpurohit, N. Lyskova, E. Churazov, W. Forman, I. Khabibullin, R. Kraft, L. Di Mascolo, T. Mroczkowski, A. Botteon, C. Jones, E. O'Sullivan, C. Zhang, R. J. van Weeren, I. Zhuravleva, G. Schellenberger, J. M. Vrtilek, L. P. David, R. Sunyaev, M. Devlin, S. Dicker, S. Haridas, J. van Marrewijk, B. S. Mason, E. Moravec, J. Orlowski-Scherer, C. Romero, C. L. Sarazin, J. Sievers
papers.abstract: The Peanut galaxy cluster (SRGe CL0238.3+2005) offers a rare opportunity to investigate thermal and nonthermal processes only $\sim0.1$\,Gyr after pericentric passage. We present a multi-frequency radio study of this system at $z=0.42$ using new MeerKAT and uGMRT observations, complemented by Chandra and MUSTANG-2 data. We identify two morphologically and spectrally distinct radio components: a double-lobed source in the northern subcluster and extended diffuse emission across the cluster center. The double-lobed source has a strongly curved, ultra-steep spectrum and is offset by $\sim22$\,kpc from the nearest brightest cluster galaxy. Its spectral curvature and positional offset are consistent with remnant AGN plasma that may have been displaced during the merger or reshaped by a shock. The diffuse emission extends over $\sim1$~Mpc and is classified as an ultra-steep spectrum ($\alpha=-1.77\pm0.11$ between 400\,MHz and 1.28\,GHz) radio halo. Its volume-averaged radio emissivity, $(1.1\pm0.1)\times10^{-41}$ erg s$^{-1}$ cm$^{-3}$ Hz$^{-1}$ at 1.4\,GHz, is an order of magnitude higher than the characteristic value for other halos. The radial profile of the halo is well described by a single exponential fit and its radio emission correlates tightly with the X-ray, with a best-fit slope of $1.11\pm0.05$. Chandra and MUSTANG-2 observations reveal candidate surface brightness discontinuities, with the most prominent inner feature coinciding with a region of flatter spectral index, potentially tracing localized particle (re)-acceleration. The coexistence of an extended ultra-steep spectrum radio halo, high radio emissivity, remnant AGN plasma, and candidate X-ray/SZ discontinuities makes the Peanut cluster an important test case for understanding the evolution of diffuse radio emission and its connection to the dynamical state of the intracluster medium in early-stage mergers.

conclusions: A $\sim 1\text{ Mpc}$ diffuse radio halo is detected across the cluster center with an ultra-steep power-law spectrum ($\alpha = -1.77 \pm 0.11$ between $400\text{ MHz}$ and $1.28\text{ GHz}$), which is unexpected so soon ($\sim 0.1\text{ Gyr}$) after core passage since ultra-steep spectra are typically associated with late-stage, decaying merger turbulence.

The halo exhibits a single-exponential radial profile ($r_e = 93 \pm 2\text{ kpc}$) and an exceptionally high volume-averaged synchrotron emissivity of $(1.1 \pm 0.1) \times 10^{-41}\text{ erg s}^{-1}\text{ cm}^{-3}\text{ Hz}^{-1}$ at $1.4\text{ GHz}$—an order of magnitude above typical radio halos and twice that of the Bullet cluster—while its surface brightness correlates super-linearly with X-ray emission ($I_\text{radio} \propto I_\text{X}^{1.11 \pm 0.05}$), indicating strong thermal–non-thermal coupling.

A bright $\approx 190\text{ kpc}$ double-lobed radio source in the northern subcluster has a strongly curved, aged synchrotron spectrum ($\nu_\text{break} \approx 581\text{ MHz}$) and is offset by $\sim 22\text{ kpc}$ from the nearest brightest cluster galaxy, pointing to remnant AGN plasma stripped or reshaped by the merger.

Chandra X-ray and MUSTANG-2 thermal SZ residual maps reveal three arc-like candidate surface brightness discontinuities, the innermost of which coincides with a localized flattening of the radio spectral index that likely traces shock-driven particle re-acceleration.
ai.summary: When massive galaxy clusters collide, shocks and turbulence stir up the hot, X-ray-emitting intracluster medium (ICM) and accelerate relativistic electrons in cluster magnetic fields, producing Mpc-scale diffuse synchrotron glow known as a radio halo. The "Peanut cluster" ($z=0.42$, $M_{500}\simeq 10^{15}\,M_\odot$) is a rare Bullet-cluster-like system caught just $\sim 0.1\text{ Gyr}$ after a nearly head-on core passage ("pericentric passage"). Using multi-frequency radio observations from MeerKAT, uGMRT, and LOFAR alongside Chandra X-ray and GBT/MUSTANG-2 thermal Sunyaev–Zeldovich (SZ) data, the authors map the non-thermal and thermal gas components during this fleeting early merger phase. They discover both a displaced remnant of dead active galactic nucleus (AGN) radio lobes and a remarkably luminous, ultra-steep spectrum radio halo, challenging standard turbulent re-acceleration models that usually predict such steep radio spectra only in much older, fading mergers.

papers.title: Calibration requirements for Epoch of Reionization 21-cm signal observations - V. Bias and variance in the cylindrical power spectrum from uGMRT Band 3 observations of the ELAIS-N1 field
papers.authors: Saikat Gayen, Suvam Tripathy, Saqueb Tanveer, Prasun Dutta, Abhik Ghosh, Khandakar Md Asif Elahi, Sarvesh Mangla, Nirupam Roy, Samir Choudhuri, Somnath Bharadwaj, Sk Saiyad Ali, Jais Kumar, Srijita Pal, Arnab Chaktaborty, Rashmi Sagar, Abhirup Datta
papers.abstract: Detection of the redshifted 21-cm signal from neutral hydrogen requires precise control of systematic effects arising from instrumental calibration. In this work, we investigate the impact of both time- and frequency-dependent residual gain and bandpass errors on the estimation of the multifrequency angular power spectrum (MAPS) using radio interferometric observations. We discuss our previously developed analytical framework for estimating bias and excess variance in 21-cm signal MAPS in the presence of these residual errors and apply it to uGMRT Band-3 observations. The statistical properties of the residual gains are derived from the data themselves, including their temporal and spectral correlations. We introduce a robust technique for additionally flagging poor-quality data. Our results show that the excess variance induced by residual gain and bandpass errors dominates over the bias across the range of angular multipoles considered. The amplitude of this variance is comparable to the expected power spectrum upper limit at redshift $z \sim 2.2$, indicating that residual calibration errors can significantly affect the detectability of the 21-cm signal. We further transform the estimated MAPS into ($k_{\perp}, k_{ll}$) space and find the expected foreground wedge structure. Importantly, we observe a significant power leakage into the nominal EoR window, which we attribute to residual calibration systematics. This highlights that even after standard foreground mitigation, time- and frequency-correlated gain errors can introduce mode-mixing and contaminate the EoR window. Our results emphasise the necessity of improved calibration accuracy and robust characterisation of residual gain statistics for current and upcoming interferometric experiments such as the uGMRT and SKA, to enable reliable detection of the cosmological 21-cm signal.

conclusions: Residual time-dependent gain and frequency-dependent bandpass errors in the uGMRT Band 3 data are well-approximated by Gaussian distributions, though their imaginary (phase) components remain correlated up to $\sim 15\text{ s}$ in time and $\sim 1.5\text{ MHz}$ in frequency.

Across all angular multipoles $\ell$ and frequency separations $\Delta\nu$, the excess variance (random scatter) induced by these residual calibration errors dominates over the systematic bias (mean offset) and is comparable in amplitude to current 21-cm upper limits at $z \sim 2.2$.

While the deterministic bias remains largely confined inside the foreground wedge in $(k_\perp, k_\parallel)$ space, the calibration-induced excess variance leaks significantly into the otherwise clean "EoR window," directly limiting the sensitivity of single-realisation sky observations.

Using a cross-polarisation estimator (Cross-TGE) further suppresses the systematic bias across $(k_\perp, k_\parallel)$, but leaves the dominant excess variance nearly unchanged, showing that reducing calibration scatter is more critical for uGMRT than removing a mean offset.
ai.summary: Mapping the cosmological 21-cm spin-flip transition of neutral hydrogen (HI) using radio interferometers is a promising way to trace large-scale structure, but astrophysical foregrounds are several orders of magnitude brighter than the signal. Normally, smooth foregrounds are confined to a "foreground wedge" in cylindrical Fourier space $(k_\perp, k_\parallel)$, leaving a clean "EoR window" for cosmology; however, tiny uncalibrated fluctuations in telescope antenna gains over time and frequency (bandpass) can mix modes and leak foreground power into this clean window. In this paper, the authors apply an analytical framework to archival uGMRT Band 3 ($300\text{--}500\text{ MHz}$, corresponding to $z \sim 2.2$) observations of the ELAIS-N1 field to empirically measure residual time- and frequency-dependent calibration errors and propagate them into the multifrequency angular power spectrum (MAPS) and cylindrical power spectrum. They show that the random scatter (excess variance) from these residual calibration errors dominates over the systematic mean offset (bias) and leaks significantly into the clean cosmological window, demonstrating that tighter control of calibration scatter is essential for 21-cm detections with uGMRT and the upcoming SKA.

papers.title: Radial dependence of galaxy and halo properties in cosmic voids: SDSS DR7 and the ELUCID constrained simulation
papers.authors: Youcai Zhang
papers.abstract: Cosmic voids provide a setting for examining the interplay between mass and environment in shaping galaxy and halo properties. Using the SDSS DR7 volume-limited galaxy sample and the ELUCID constrained simulation of the local large-scale structure, we investigate the radial profiles of galaxy and subhalo properties across different mass ranges, identifying voids independently in the observed galaxy and simulated subhalo distributions. Both stellar mass and subhalo mass increase from void interiors toward the void boundary, indicating that lower-mass galaxies and subhaloes preferentially reside in void interiors. The satellite fraction of subhaloes also increases systematically toward the void boundary. Galaxy colour and specific star formation rate exhibit radial variations that are weaker than their dependence on stellar mass, while the spiral fraction shows little radial dependence at fixed stellar mass. For dark-matter haloes, the apparent radial increase in size within a broad high-mass bin largely disappears when narrower mass ranges are considered. Halo concentration and spin show radial variations at fixed mass, with higher concentrations and lower spins toward void interiors, although the concentration trend is less pronounced in the extended low-mass sample. The formation redshift of low-mass subhaloes also increases toward the void boundary, whereas this dependence weakens and eventually disappears at higher masses. Overall, the radial trends in galaxy properties are generally weaker than their mass dependence, while several subhalo properties retain measurable radial variations at fixed mass.

conclusions: Both observed galaxy stellar mass and simulated dark-matter subhalo mass show clear mass segregation inside cosmic voids, with mean stellar mass increasing by about $0.12\text{ dex}$ (from $\log(M_*/h^{-2}M_\odot) \simeq 10.38$ near void centres to $\simeq 10.50$ at the boundary $r/R_{\rm v}=1$) and remaining flat outside.

Once galaxy samples are split into narrow stellar-mass bins, apparent radial trends in galaxy morphology (spiral fraction) and size ($R_{50}$) largely vanish, showing they are mainly artifacts of mass segregation; only weak residual trends remain for colour and specific star formation rate (sSFR), with inner-void galaxies being slightly bluer and more actively star-forming.

Unlike galaxies, dark-matter subhaloes in ELUCID retain genuine environmental dependencies at fixed mass (assembly bias): inner-void haloes have higher concentrations (for $M_{\rm sub} \ge 10^{11.8}\,h^{-1}M_\odot$) and systematically lower dimensionless spin parameters ($\lambda$) than those near void walls.

Low-mass subhaloes ($M_{\rm sub} < 10^{12.3}\,h^{-1}M_\odot$) in void interiors form more recently (lower formation redshift $z_{\rm f}$) and have a near-zero satellite fraction compared to those near the boundary, whereas high-mass subhaloes show no significant radial variation in formation time.

ai.summary: Galaxies residing in cosmic voids generally look smaller, bluer, and more star-forming than those in denser filaments and walls, but a longstanding question in galaxy evolution is whether the underdense void environment directly alters how galaxies grow, or if voids simply host lower-mass dark matter haloes (which naturally host smaller, bluer galaxies). To disentangle true environmental effects from this mass segregation, the author compares a volume-limited sample of ~159,000 galaxies from SDSS DR7 with the ELUCID constrained N-body simulation—a dark-matter simulation whose initial density field was reconstructed to reproduce the actual local Universe's large-scale structure. Identifying ~400 voids in both datasets using the watershed-based REVOLVER algorithm, they measure radial profiles of galaxy and subhalo properties as a function of normalized distance from the void centre ($r/R_{\rm v}$) within narrow mass bins. This side-by-side analysis reveals that while most observable galaxy trends inside voids are driven simply by stellar-mass segregation, the underlying dark matter subhaloes retain genuine, mass-independent environmental imprints in their assembly histories and internal dynamics.

papers.title: Cracking into RACS - I. Measuring the cosmic dipole in the RACS-low3 and RACS-mid1 radio surveys with simulation-based inference
papers.authors: Oliver T. Oayda, Mali Land-Strykowski, Stefan W. Duchesne, Emil Lenc, Tara Murphy, Geraint F. Lewis
papers.abstract: We measure the dipole in the count of radio galaxies over the sky as seen by the Australian SKA Pathfinder (ASKAP) in the Rapid ASKAP Continuum Survey (RACS). Our analysis focuses on the third observational epoch in the 'low' passband (943.5 MHz; RACS-low3) and the first epoch in the 'mid' passband (1367.5 MHz; RACS-mid1). We find strong evidence for a systematic relation between flux density and the temperature at the time of observation, whereby reported flux densities are suppressed to a greater degree when the ASKAP antennas are warmer. We include this temperature response in our forward model as part of our Simulation-based Inference (SBI) pipeline, generating data realisations that are then used by a neural network to learn the likelihood function. Despite this model, RACS-low3 and RACS-mid1 both exhibit a dipole inconsistent with the kinematic dipole of the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB), adding further evidence for the 'cosmic dipole tension'. For RACS-low3, the dipole agrees in direction but has an amplitude four times in excess, while the dipole for RACS-mid1 is offset from the CMB and has an amplitude roughly five times in excess. Our findings underscore the importance of interrogating the data for systematic effects and showcase the power of SBI in handling them.

conclusions: Even after correcting for instrumental systematics, RACS-low3 exhibits a dipole direction consistent with the CMB ($\ln\mathcal{B} = 2.3 \pm 0.5$) but an inferred observer velocity $4.03^{+0.72}_{-0.71}$ times the CMB expectation ($\approx 1490\text{ km s}^{-1}$ vs. $370\text{ km s}^{-1}$), reinforcing the cosmic dipole tension.

Accounting for the receiver temperature response is critical for RACS-low3 ($\ln\mathcal{B} = -37.6 \pm 1.1$ when omitted); ignoring it artificially inflates the inferred velocity to $9.57^{+0.46}_{-0.43}$ times the CMB value because hot daytime observations systematically suppress flux counts.

RACS-mid1 yields a dipole amplitude roughly $5$ times the CMB expectation (or $3.42^{+0.96}_{-0.98}$ times when fixed to the CMB direction), but its direction is strongly pulled toward the north equatorial pole ($\ln\mathcal{B} = -9.6 \pm 0.5$ against alignment with the CMB) due to remaining unmodelled declination-dependent striping systematics.

Models assuming pure Poisson noise are decisively ruled out ($\ln\mathcal{B} = -83.2$ for low3 and $-130.5$ for mid1), proving that accounting for source overdispersion/clustering (such as multi-component radio galaxies split by source-finders) is essential for accurate one-point statistics.
ai.relevance_reason: Directly applies simulation-based inference (SBI) to test the cosmological principle and large-scale isotropy via the cosmic dipole tension, connecting to both SBI methodologies and observational tests of inhomogeneous/anisotropic cosmologies.
ai.summary: Under the cosmological principle, distant galaxies should be isotropically distributed in the cosmic rest frame, meaning our solar system's motion through space should imprint a kinematic dipole in galaxy number counts across the sky (the Ellis–Baldwin test) that matches the direction and speed ($v \approx 370\text{ km s}^{-1}$) of the CMB temperature dipole. However, radio and infrared surveys consistently find a number-count dipole several times larger than expected—a puzzle known as the "cosmic dipole tension." In this paper, the authors measure the radio galaxy dipole in two epochs of the Rapid ASKAP Continuum Survey (RACS-low3 at $943.5\text{ MHz}$ and RACS-mid1 at $1367.5\text{ MHz}$) using Simulation-Based Inference (SBI), where a neural network learns the likelihood from forward-simulated sky maps. Crucially, their forward model incorporates pseudo-clustering of sources and a newly identified instrumental systematic: when the telescope's phased-array feed (PAF) receivers heat up during hot daytime observations, reported source flux densities are systematically suppressed. This work matters because it demonstrates how forward modelling and SBI can disentangle subtle hardware and survey systematics from genuine cosmological signals in large-scale structure tests.

papers.title: Model-independent calibration of gamma-ray bursts with Bayesian neural networks
papers.authors: P. Caterino, M.Demianski, E. Piedipalumbo, L. Amati, D. De Cicco, M. Brescia
papers.abstract: Context. Gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) extend cosmological distance measurements beyond the range densely sampled by Type Ia supernovae, but their standardization requires reliable calibration and uncertainty estimates. Aims. We calibrate the Amati correlation without assuming a background cosmological model, assess its stability, and examine the cosmological reach of current and future GRB Hubble diagrams. Methods. We train a Bayesian neural network on Pantheon+ supernovae, assess and recalibrate its predictive uncertainties, and calibrate the correlation for GRBs at $z \leq 1.5$ using the D'Agostini and Reichart likelihoods. We combine the GRB Hubble diagram with supernovae, Hubble-parameter measurements, and DESI baryon acoustic oscillations. Local-regression, covariance, leave-three-out, redshift-evolution, and Efron-Petrosian diagnostics test the standardization assumptions. We also analyse idealized future catalogues of 1500 standardized GRBs. Results. The diagram reaches $z \simeq 9.4$. Covariance and leave-three-out diagnostics produce small changes in the cosmological constraints. A parametric evolution coefficient is consistent with zero, whereas the truncation-corrected diagnostic indicates marginal isotropic-energy evolution that can occur along the Amati relation. Dark-energy extensions improve the phenomenological fit relative to flat $\Lambda$CDM: AIC favours the Chevallier-Polarski-Linder parametrization, while BIC favours constant-$w$ dark energy. Forecasts show strong conditional model-discrimination power under the adopted uncertainty model. Conclusions. GRBs provide a complementary high-redshift extension of the supernova distance ladder. Present results do not establish an evolving dark-energy equation of state. Larger homogeneous samples are promising, but realistic selection functions and calibration systematics remain essential.

conclusions: Calibrating the Amati relation ($E_{\rm iso}$ vs. $E_{\rm p,i}$) using the BNN distance reconstruction yields an intercept $b \approx 52.85$, a slope $a = 2.13^{+0.24}_{-0.20}$ (Reichart likelihood; $1.67 \pm 0.17$ for D'Agostini), and a substantial intrinsic log-scatter of $\sigma_{\rm int} \approx 0.44\text{--}0.47$ dex that dominates individual GRB distance uncertainties.

Explicit post-hoc uncertainty recalibration on the BNN test set reduces the miscalibration area from $0.09$ to $0.02$ and cuts the mean predictive variance in half ($0.264 \to 0.126$), providing reliable error bars to anchor 264 long GRBs out to $z \simeq 9.4$.

Redshift-evolution and selection diagnostics show no significant evolution perpendicular to the Amati relation, though truncation-corrected Efron–Petrosian tests indicate marginal evolution of $E_{\rm iso}$ *along* the relation due to flux limits.

Combining the GRB Hubble diagram with Pantheon+, $H(z)$ data, and DESI BAO improves phenomenological fits over flat $\Lambda$CDM, but model selection remains inconclusive: AIC favors evolving dark energy ($w_0 w_a$ / CPL) while the more stringent BIC favors constant-$w$ dark energy.
ai.relevance_reason: Loosely relevant as background on combining DESI BAO and Pantheon+ SNe with high-redshift probes to test dynamical dark energy ($w_0 w_a$), alongside machine-learning uncertainty calibration techniques.
ai.summary: Gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) are ultra-luminous explosions visible out to $z \simeq 9.4$, making them an attractive tool for extending the cosmological distance ladder well beyond the reach of Type Ia supernovae (SNIa, $z \lesssim 2.3$). Because GRBs are not standard candles, they must be standardized via empirical scaling laws like the Amati relation—which links a burst's rest-frame spectral peak energy ($E_{\rm p,i}$) to its total isotropic-equivalent radiated energy ($E_{\rm iso}$)—without assuming a cosmological model beforehand (which would create a circularity problem). The authors train a Bayesian neural network (BNN) with Concrete Dropout on the Pantheon+ SNIa sample (incorporating the full SN covariance matrix and explicitly recalibrating predictive uncertainties) to reconstruct a model-independent distance-modulus curve at $z \le 1.5$. They use this curve to anchor the Amati relation for a sample of 264 long GRBs, build an extended Hubble diagram up to $z \simeq 9.4$, and combine it with Pantheon+, cosmic chronometers, and DESI BAO to test dark energy models and forecasts for future surveys like THESEUS.

papers.title: pbhalo: computing primordial black hole and minihalo populations from a single primordial perturbation spectrum
papers.authors: B.A. Rudenko
papers.abstract: An enhancement of the primordial curvature power spectrum on small scales can give rise to two populations of compact objects: primordial black holes (PBHs), which form during radiation domination, and dark matter minihalos, including ultracompact minihalos (UCMHs), which form from the same modes during matter domination. We present pbhalo, an open-source Python package that computes the PBH mass function, the halo mass function and the UCMH abundance from a single spectrum in a given cosmology and applies observational constraints on the PBH abundance and on the spectrum jointly. The package components are validated against colossus (a code for halo mass functions and cosmological quantities), pbhstat (a code for the PBH mass function from a given spectrum) and published results; joint constraints are illustrated for lognormal peaks. The code is distributed under the MIT license.

conclusions: Using a real-space top-hat filter for spectra with a sharp small-scale peak causes high-$k$ power to leak into low masses, overpredicting the halo mass function by a factor of $14$–$38$ at $M \sim 10^{-6}$–$10^{-5}\,M_\odot$ ($z=30$) compared to smooth-$k$ filters.

Applying scale-invariant UCMH bounds directly to the peak of a lognormal feature ($w=0.5$) overstates the constraint on the integrated peak amplitude $A$ by a factor of $1.5$–$1.8$, whereas evaluating the Carr et al. extended mass function criterion on combined class envelopes rather than individual bounds over-tightens $A$ by up to a factor of $10$.

For $1.6 \times 10^3 \lesssim k_p/\mathrm{Mpc}^{-1} \lesssim 10^{12}$, observational PBH bounds limit a lognormal peak ($w=0.5$) to $A \simeq (0.9\text{--}2.5) \times 10^{-2}$ (assuming non-linear compaction, which raises the required $A$ by a factor of $\simeq 2$ compared to linear compaction), while CMB $\mu$-distortions constrain $A \lesssim (4\text{--}5) \times 10^{-5}$ at $k_p \lesssim 2 \times 10^3\,\mathrm{Mpc}^{-1}$.

If dark matter annihilates, the UCMH bound ($f_{\rm UCMH} < 10^{-5}$) restricts the peak amplitude to $A \lesssim (1.6\text{--}13) \times 10^{-7}$ across $10^2 \le k_p/\mathrm{Mpc}^{-1} \lesssim 1.6 \times 10^7$—up to $5 \times 10^4$ times stronger than other probes—implying that producing an appreciable PBH population without violating UCMH limits requires either non-annihilating dark matter or a peak at $k_p \gtrsim 3 \times 10^7\,\mathrm{Mpc}^{-1}$ ($M_{\rm PBH} \lesssim 10^{-2}\,M_\odot$).
ai.summary: While the primordial curvature power spectrum $\Delta^2_\zeta(k)$ is tightly constrained to $\sim 2 \times 10^{-9}$ on large CMB scales, many inflationary models predict strong enhancements on much smaller scales ($k \gg 1\,\mathrm{Mpc}^{-1}$). Depending on the amplitude, these small-scale peaks can form two distinct populations of compact objects: primordial black holes (PBHs), which collapse when extreme density fluctuations ($\Delta^2_\zeta \gtrsim 10^{-2}$) re-enter the horizon during radiation domination, and ultracompact minihalos (UCMHs), which are dense, early-forming ($z \sim 10^2$–$10^3$) dark matter halos seeded during matter domination by weaker enhancements ($10^{-7} \lesssim \Delta^2_\zeta \lesssim 10^{-2}$). Because existing public codes treat PBHs and halo mass functions separately—often with inconsistent window functions, growth normalizations, or scale-invariant approximations—the author introduces `pbhalo`, an open-source Python package that consistently computes PBH mass functions, standard minihalo mass functions, and UCMH abundances from a single arbitrary $\Delta^2_\zeta(k)$ across matter-radiation equality. The package integrates 34 observational PBH bounds, integral CMB $\mu$-distortion limits (early spectral distortions from acoustic damping), and UCMH bounds to map out joint constraints on small-scale primordial features.

papers.title: Dark Matter and MOND successes and degeneracies in reproducing SPARC rotation curves and weak lensing data
papers.authors: Amy Smith, Francesco Shankar, Daeun Jeong, Nicola Menci, Andrea Lapi, Hao Fu, Xinyu Dai, Mariangela Bernardi, Arianna Di Cintio, Annagrazia Puglisi, Alexander Belyaev, Hendrik Ulbricht, Ivette Fuentes-Guridi
papers.abstract: The observed rotation velocities of spiral galaxies at large scales exceed those predicted by their baryonic components, motivating the need for dark matter (DM) or Modified Newtonian Dynamics (MOND). We fit the rotation curves of 147 late-type galaxies from the SPARC database, using a suite of models including Cold Dark Matter (CDM) models with and without baryonic feedback, Warm DM, Fuzzy DM, and MOND. We also combine SPARC kinematics with weak-lensing data to extend the mean rotation curves to ~1 Mpc. On a galaxy-by-galaxy basis, the inner SPARC rotation curves marginally favour CDM models with baryonic feedback, although accounting for the uncertainties in distances and inclinations increases the degeneracy among DM-based models and MOND. All DM models predict host halo masses larger than abundance-matching expectations, with only the CDM model with baryonic feedback reducing the scatter around the mean luminosity-halo mass relation. MOND is able to reproduce the flatness of the mean galactic rotation curves on scales up to 1 Mpc, providing stellar mass-to-light ratios within observational uncertainties. In contrast, all DM models, without the contribution of mass external to the bound halo, struggle to explain the flat rotation curves. The inclusion of the current weak-lensing data tends to favour MOND over DM models, at least at the largest scales. Future observations from BIG-SPARC, the Square Kilometre Array, and most importantly, upcoming weak-lensing surveys such as EUCLID and Rubin will provide more stringent and independent tests of these competing frameworks

conclusions: On individual SPARC galaxy rotation curves, the baryonic feedback CDM model (DC14) achieves the best overall fit with a median reduced chi-squared of $\chi^2_\nu = 0.934$ (fixed distance and inclination), and is strongly preferred by the Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC) in $\sim 33\%$ of the full sample ($\sim 40\text{--}50\%$ for dwarf galaxies).

Accounting for observational uncertainties in galaxy distances and inclinations significantly reduces the $\chi^2_\nu$ discrepancy between MOND and dark matter models, demonstrating strong parameter degeneracies between the MOND acceleration scale $a_0$, stellar mass-to-light ratio $\Upsilon_*$, and geometric nuisance parameters.

All tested dark matter halo profiles systematically infer host halo masses ($M_{\rm vir}$) larger than predicted by $3.6\,\mu\text{m}$ abundance matching; only the DC14 baryonic feedback model substantially reduces the scatter around the mean luminosity–halo mass relation.

When extending mean rotation curves out to $\sim 1\,\text{Mpc}$ using stacked KiDS weak-lensing data, MOND naturally reproduces the observed flat circular velocities across all mass bins, whereas isolated dark matter halo models decline too rapidly beyond the virial radius unless unbound external mass (e.g., the two-halo term) is included.
ai.relevance_reason: Provides useful background on galactic-scale tests of modified gravity (MOND) versus dark matter profiles and galaxy-galaxy weak lensing, though it focuses on analytic halo profile fitting rather than cosmological simulations or large-scale structure emulators.
ai.summary: The flat rotation curves of spiral galaxies can be explained either by embedding galaxies in extended dark matter (DM) haloes or by modifying Newtonian dynamics below a critical acceleration scale $a_0 \approx 1.2 \times 10^{-10}\,\text{m}\,\text{s}^{-2}$ (MOND). In this paper, the authors perform a uniform MCMC comparison across 147 late-type galaxies from the SPARC database (which combines $3.6\,\mu\text{m}$ Spitzer photometry with $\text{H}\alpha/\text{H}\,\text{I}$ gas kinematics), testing standard cuspy NFW profiles, cored baryonic-feedback CDM profiles (DC14), Warm DM, Fuzzy DM (ultralight axions with solitonic cores), and Modified Inertia MOND. They further test how well these models obey global scaling relations via abundance matching (linking galaxy luminosities to theoretical halo mass functions) and append stacked galaxy-galaxy weak lensing data from KiDS to probe average circular velocities out to $\sim 1\,\text{Mpc}$—well beyond typical halo virial radii. This unified analysis across scales highlights a regime split: cored CDM with baryonic feedback best captures the diversity of inner rotation curves, while MOND naturally explains the persistent flatness of weak-lensing rotation curves at megaparsec scales where isolated DM halo profiles drop off.

papers.title: SN Ares: A Strongly Lensed Type IIb Supernova at $\mathbf{z=1.276}$ with a Predicted 70-Year Time Delay
papers.authors: Conor Larison, Justin D. R. Pierel, Matthew Siebert, Tom Resseguier, Lukas J. Furtak, Masamune Oguri, Gavin S. Farley, Hollis B. Akins, Yoshihisa Asada, Rachel Bezanson, Maruša Bradač, Gabriel Brammer, John Chisholm, Dan Coe, Pratika Dayal, Henry C. Ferguson, Steven L. Finkelstein, Seiji Fujimoto, Tomokazu Kiyota, Anton M. papers.abstract: We present the discovery of supernova (SN) Ares, a strongly lensed supernova at $z_{\rm spec}=1.276\pm0.002$ in a massive, triply imaged host galaxy behind the MACS J0308.9+2645 galaxy cluster. JWST/NIRSpec spectroscopy spanning the rest-frame optical to NIR of Ares reveals helium features at $5876\,\mathring{\mathrm{A}}$, $7065\,\mathring{\mathrm{A}}$, and $10830\,\mathring{\mathrm{A}}$, as well as H$\alpha$ and Pa$\beta$. A comparison to local core-collapse SN spectra and light curves leads to a classification of SN Ares as a Type IIb supernova, the highest-redshift member of its class spectroscopically identified. A comparison to local SN IIb light curves provides a phase estimate for the spectrum of $34_{-9}^{+10}$ rest-frame days post-radioactive peak, providing a unique view into a high-redshift stripped-envelope supernova in its late-photospheric evolution. A lens model of the cluster constructed using recent JWST data indicates that SN Ares is the first image to arrive and will reappear in two future images near the center of the cluster plane in $\gtrsim 70$ years, with predicted magnifications of $\sim5\times$ and $\sim1.5\times$. Planned JWST/NIRSpec Multi-Object Spectroscopy of the cluster will allow for more detailed modeling of the lensed system for tighter constraints on the time delay and magnifications, as well as a template spectrum at the location of SN Ares.

conclusions: Spectroscopic analysis and light-curve template matching classify SN Ares as a Type IIb supernova caught at $34^{+10}_{-9}$ rest-frame days after peak brightness, making it the highest-redshift spectroscopically confirmed SN IIb to date.

Correcting for a lensing magnification of $\mu \approx 5.6 \pm 0.5$ ($\sim 1.9$ mag boost), the inferred peak $B$-band absolute magnitude is between $-17.1$ and $-17.9$ mag, matching normal local SN IIb explosions (such as SN 1993J) and suggesting a binary progenitor origin.

Assuming $H_0 = 70\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}}$, cluster lens models (Lenstool, glafic, and AstroLensPy) predict that the second and third images of SN Ares will arrive in $\sim 70\text{--}73$ and $\sim 73\text{--}77$ years with magnifications of $\mu \approx 4.9$ and $\mu \approx 1.5$, respectively.

Because a $3\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}}$ shift in $H_0$ alters the predicted arrival time by roughly 5 years, eventually observing the reappearance of SN Ares would yield a sub-percent fractional time-delay uncertainty, leaving cluster lens mass modeling as the primary systematic for $H_0$.

ai.summary: When a massive galaxy cluster acts as a strong gravitational lens for a background supernova (SN), light travels along multiple paths of different lengths and gravitational potentials, creating multiple magnified images that arrive at different times. Measuring these arrival-time delays provides a direct geometric distance measurement to constrain the Hubble constant ($H_0$, via "time-delay cosmography"), while the lensing magnification allows us to study faint, high-redshift SN explosions in detail. In this paper, the authors report the JWST discovery and follow-up of SN Ares at $z_{\rm spec} = 1.276 \pm 0.002$ behind the galaxy cluster MACS J0308.9+2645, using NIRCam difference imaging and NIRSpec spectroscopy alongside three independent cluster mass models. They identify SN Ares as a Type IIb supernova—a core-collapse explosion whose progenitor star had most of its outer hydrogen envelope stripped away, leaving prominent helium and residual hydrogen lines—and predict that two trailing images of the explosion will appear near the cluster core in roughly 70 years. This makes SN Ares both the most distant spectroscopically confirmed Type IIb supernova and the longest-baseline time-delay cosmography system known.

papers.title: Initial Conditions of Magnetized AGN Accretion Disks from Cloud Capture and Disruption
papers.authors: Philip F. Hopkins
papers.abstract: Accretion onto supermassive black holes (BHs) from the ISM can occur via capture of cold gas 'clouds' (GMCs, clumps, or overdense structures). Unlike material in stellar tidal disruptions or X-ray binaries, or classical Bondi accretion, ISM clouds are strongly magnetized (plasma $\beta \equiv P_{\rm thermal}/P_{\rm magnetic} \ll 1$), with supersonic turbulence, and cool rapidly. We derive analytic scalings for the initial conditions of accretion disks formed by capture/disruption of such clouds, in three regimes: (1) low-mass BHs ($M_{\rm BH} \ll M_{\rm cl}$), where turbulent Bondi-Hoyle or hierarchical 'leapfrog' growth via sub-cloud encounters dominates; (2) comparable-mass encounters ($M_{\rm BH} \sim M_{\rm cl}$); and (3) massive BHs tidally disrupting small clouds ($M_{\rm BH} \gg M_{\rm cl}$). In each, the resulting disk is predicted to be initially toroidally-magnetically-dominated ($|B_{\phi}| \gg |B_{z}|$, $\beta \ll 1$), geometrically thick ($H/R \sim 0.1-1$), and gravitationally stable ($Q \gtrsim 1$), with super-sonic, trans-Alfvenic turbulence. These conditions differ qualitatively from those assumed in classical accretion/$\alpha$ disk theory, 'chaotic cold accretion', stellar tidal disruption, or Bondi-Hoyle accretion. At least initially, the toroidal field should be sustained by flux-freezing on timescales shorter than Parker or turbulent resistive losses. We examine how cloud mass spectra drive accretion rate distributions, duty cycles, and fueling rates, with integrated BH growth dominated by clouds of mass comparable to the BH. Given known cosmological evolution, we suggest a scenario linking (a) inefficient growth and wandering BHs in dwarf galaxies, (b) hyper-Eddington growth in little red dots, (c) peak quasar activity in massive gas-rich systems at cosmic noon, and (d) lower-luminosity AGN in gas-poor galaxies at late times.

conclusions: Across all black hole-to-cloud mass regimes, the newly formed outer accretion disk is strongly magnetically dominated ($\beta_d \lesssim \beta_{\rm cl} \ll 1$) with amplified toroidal fields ($|B_\phi| \gg |B_z|, |B_R|$), geometrically thick ($H/R \sim 0.1\text{--}1$ supported by magnetic pressure), and gravitationally stable (Toomre $Q_d \gg 1$).

The time-averaged accretion rate, encounter rate, and duty cycle are dominated by clouds with masses comparable to the black hole ($M_{\rm cl} \sim M_{\rm BH}$), which naturally trigger vigorous accretion at or above the Eddington limit.

The disk accretion rate scales with cloud surface density as $\dot{M}_d \propto \Sigma_{\rm cl}^{3/4}$ (and $\dot{M}_d \propto M_{\rm cl}^{3/4}$ for $M_{\rm cl} \lesssim M_{\rm BH}$ or $\propto M_{\rm cl}^{-1/4}$ for $M_{\rm cl} \gtrsim M_{\rm BH}$), resembling a Shu-like isothermal collapse rather than classical Bondi ($\propto M_{\rm BH}^2$) or viscous $\alpha$-disk scalings.

For low-mass black holes ($M_{\rm BH} \ll M_{\rm cl}$), smooth turbulent Bondi-Hoyle capture is inefficient, but encounters with dense internal sub-clouds ($M_{\rm cl}^{\rm sub} \sim M_{\rm BH}$) enable rapid, episodic "leapfrog" growth that can connect seed black holes in dwarf galaxies to hyper-Eddington "little red dots" and cosmic noon quasars.

Classical accretion theories (like Bondi-Hoyle accretion, stellar tidal disruption events, or standard Shakura–Sunyaev $\alpha$-disks) assume the incoming gas is dominated by thermal pressure rather than magnetic pressure (high plasma $\beta \equiv P_{\rm thermal}/P_{\rm magnetic} \gg 1$) and cools slowly, whereas real ISM clouds are strongly magnetized ($\beta \ll 1$), supersonically turbulent, and cool rapidly. In this paper, Hopkins derives analytic scaling relations for the outer boundary ("initial") conditions of accretion disks formed when black holes capture and circularize such magnetized, turbulent clouds across three mass regimes ($M_{\rm BH} \ll M_{\rm cl}$, $M_{\rm BH} \sim M_{\rm cl}$, and $M_{\rm BH} \gg M_{\rm cl}$) and integrates them over an observed ISM cloud mass spectrum. He shows that flux-freezing during capture amplifies the azimuthal magnetic field, creating thick, gravitationally stable, magnetically supported disks whose fueling rates are dominated by clouds with masses comparable to the black hole—offering a unified physical framework for black hole growth from dwarf galaxies to bright quasars.

papers.title: Constraining Ultralight Dark Matter in Dynamical Dark Energy Cosmologies
papers.authors: Muhammad Awais, Hafiz Inam Ullah, Rafael C. Nunes, Paula S. Ferreira, Tonatiuh Matos
papers.abstract: We investigate the cosmological implications of scalar-field dark matter (SFDM) in a dynamical dark energy framework, extending previous analyses that considered SFDM within the standard $\Lambda$CDM cosmological model. We consistently implement the scenario at both the background and linear perturbation levels. We perform Bayesian parameter inference using Planck CMB measurements, DESI DR2 baryon acoustic oscillation (BAO) data, and Pantheon+ Type Ia supernovae to constrain the model parameter space. Our theoretical predictions show that lighter scalar-field masses produce increasingly strong scale-dependent suppression of matter fluctuations and more pronounced modifications to the CMB temperature power spectrum, whereas heavier masses progressively approach the cold dark matter limit. For the SFDM mass, we obtain a one-sided 95\% lower limit of $\log_{10}(m_\phi/{\rm eV})>-24.04$ from our main joint analysis. We find that replacing the standard cold dark matter fluid with SFDM does not qualitatively alter the constraints on dynamical dark energy or the evidence for its evolution, including a phantom crossing at low redshifts.

conclusions: Replacing CDM with ultralight scalar-field dark matter does not shift the inferred background parameters or the preference for evolving dark energy: Planck + DESI DR2 yields $H_0 = 65.37 \pm 1.39\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}}$, $\Omega_m = 0.3327 \pm 0.0153$, and $S_8 = 0.8319 \pm 0.0156$.

The dark energy transition parameters remain robust at $\Delta = -0.2304 \pm 0.0981$ and $z_\dagger = 0.5127 \pm 0.0830$, corresponding to a phantom-to-quintessence crossing ($w_x$ going from $<-1$ at higher redshift to $>-1$ today) around $z \approx 0.5$.

The scalar-field mass is bounded from below at $\log_{10}(m_\phi/\mathrm{eV}) > -24.11$ (Planck + DESI DR2) and $> -24.04$ (adding Pantheon+) at 95% confidence, ruling out the lightest masses that would overly suppress large-scale structure while recovering standard CDM behavior at higher masses.

This paper asks whether combining these two beyond-$\Lambda$CDM ideas—replacing CDM with a quadratic scalar field $V(\phi) = \frac{1}{2}m_\phi^2\phi^2$ inside a dynamical dark energy model featuring a smooth late-time equation-of-state transition ($w_\dagger$VCDM, where VCDM is a minimalist modified gravity framework that alters the background expansion and linear momentum constraint without adding propagating dark energy perturbations)—changes the observational evidence for evolving dark energy. papers.title: Catastrophe Structure and Stability of Axion Stars
papers.authors: Fedor V Kusmartsev, Joudy J F Beek, Jack C M Hughes
papers.abstract: Axion stars are self-gravitating Bose--Einstein condensates of QCD axions or axion-like particles. Their stability determines whether they can survive as dark-matter structures and what astrophysical signatures they may produce. Here we combine a non-relativistic Schrödinger--Poisson description with catastrophe theory to develop a unified picture of axion-star stability. Beginning with the Einstein--Klein--Gordon system for a periodic axion potential, we derive the effective equations of motion and conserved quantities and construct a one-parameter family of star-like solutions. A Gaussian variational ansatz reduces the problem to an analytic energy functional $E(R;N)$. Within this model, equilibria appear and disappear through Arnold $A_2$, $A_3$, and $A_4$ catastrophes as the particle number $N$ and interaction strengths vary. A repulsive sextic interaction produces two stable branches---dilute and dense axion stars---separated by an unstable branch. The same catastrophe criteria apply beyond the sextic truncation: for the full cosine and QCD-corrected potentials, the fold conditions follow from the complete variational energy and can be evaluated numerically. We also separate stability within the collective-coordinate ansatz from full radial perturbative stability and specify the range in which the non-relativistic treatment is reliable. This framework provides a compact classification of axion-star phases and identifies model-dependent critical masses associated with collapse, bosenova-like emission, and black-hole formation.

conclusions: Using a Gaussian variational ansatz, the stability of axion stars can be mapped onto Arnold's $A_2$ (fold), $A_3$ (cusp), and $A_4$ (swallowtail) catastrophes in the energy landscape $E(R; N)$ as particle number $N$ and self-interaction strengths vary.

Adding a repulsive sextic ($\phi^6$) self-interaction creates two distinct stable equilibrium branches—low-density "dilute" stars and high-density "dense" stars—separated by an intermediate unstable branch.

The catastrophe fold criteria extend beyond polynomial truncations to the full cosine and QCD-corrected chiral potentials, allowing direct numerical determination of critical threshold masses for gravitational collapse, relativistic "bosenova" bursts of axions, and black-hole formation.

The authors explicitly distinguish stability within the simplified collective-coordinate variational ansatz from full radial perturbative stability, delineating the regime where the non-relativistic Schrödinger–Poisson approximation breaks down.
ai.summary: If dark matter is made of ultralight bosons like axions, quantum pressure and gravity can balance to form macroscopic, self-gravitating Bose–Einstein condensates known as "axion stars." Understanding when these compact objects remain stable or suddenly collapse is crucial for predicting their survival as dark matter substructures and their potential astrophysical signatures. Starting from the relativistic Einstein–Klein–Gordon equations and taking the non-relativistic Schrödinger–Poisson limit, the authors model the axion star profile with a Gaussian variational ansatz to obtain an analytic energy functional $E(R; N)$ in terms of the star's radius $R$ and particle number $N$. They then apply catastrophe theory—a mathematical framework for classifying how equilibrium points suddenly appear, merge, or vanish as control parameters change—to map out the stability phases of axion stars across polynomial, full cosine, and QCD-corrected interaction potentials. This provides a unified, analytic classification of the critical mass thresholds where axion stars transition between stable configurations, undergo "bosenova" explosions (violent emission of relativistic axions), or collapse into black holes.

papers.title: Exploring the Limits: Neutrino Mass and Interacting Dark Sector in the DESI Era
papers.authors: Weiqiang Yang, Sibo Zhang, Supriya Pan, Luis A. Anchordoqui, Eleonora Di Valentino
papers.abstract: We constrain three interacting dark matter--dark energy scenarios using cosmic microwave background measurements, DESI DR2 baryon acoustic oscillations, and the PantheonPlus, Union3, and DES-Dovekie Type Ia supernova compilations. We consider interacting vacuum energy and interacting dark energy with a constant equation of state in the phantom and quintessence regimes, analyzing each scenario with either a fixed total neutrino mass or a freely varying effective neutrino mass. When the positivity prior is relaxed, all three scenarios favor negative effective neutrino masses for every dataset combination. Although some combinations permit small positive masses, none of the 95\% confidence intervals reaches the minimum mass required by neutrino oscillation experiments. Allowing the effective neutrino mass to vary produces significances for a nonzero coupling reaching approximately $3\sigma$, but the preferred masses remain negative. These results demonstrate that the interaction and constant dark energy equations of state considered here fail to resolve the DESI neutrino-mass tension.

conclusions: Across all three interacting dark sector models (interacting vacuum with $w_x = -1$, and constant-$w_0$ phantom or quintessence regimes) and all dataset combinations, relaxing the positivity prior yields a preference for unphysical negative effective neutrino masses (e.g., $\sum m_{\nu,\mathrm{eff}} \approx -0.125$ to $-0.182\,\mathrm{eV}$ in the interacting vacuum case), and none of the $95\%$ confidence intervals reach the minimum terrestrial oscillation bound of $\sum m_\nu \ge 0.057\,\mathrm{eV}$.

Allowing $\sum m_{\nu,\mathrm{eff}}$ to vary freely alongside the dark-sector interaction boosts the statistical preference for a nonzero coupling $\xi$ up to $\sim 2\text{--}3\sigma$ (with $\xi < 0$, indicating energy transfer from dark energy to dark matter) and improves the fit by $\Delta \chi^2_{\mathrm{min}} \approx -5.4$ to $-5.9$ when supernovae are included, yet the preferred neutrino mass remains firmly negative.

Phenomenological energy transfer proportional to the Hubble expansion rate ($Q = 3\xi \mathcal{H}\rho_x$) with a constant dark energy equation of state cannot replicate the high-redshift ($z > 2.33$) dark energy suppression that enables $w_0w_a$CDM to resolve the geometric distance mismatch and relax cosmological neutrino mass bounds.

papers.title: Comment on "Effect of perfect fluid dark matter..." [Phys. Dark Univ. 34 (2021) 100891]
papers.authors: Ming-Hsun Li, Kwei-Chou Yang
papers.abstract: This Comment clarifies the physical interpretation of the black hole spacetime metric employed by Shaymatov \textit{et al.} [Phys. Dark Univ. 34 (2021) 100891]. We point out that the metric, originally derived in Li and Yang (2012), describes a specific dual-component system consisting of cold dark matter and a phantom field background. Treating this geometry as a single-component ``Perfect Fluid Dark Matter'' (PFDM) with a total equation of state $w_{\mathrm{total}} = -1$ is physically incompatible with the gravitational attraction required for dark matter halos. Furthermore, we clarify the distinct parameter regimes of the original model to prevent potential misapplications in extreme astrophysical scenarios.

conclusions: The effective radial equation of state $w_{r,\mathrm{total}} = p_r/\rho = -1$ derived from the logarithmic metric is fundamentally incompatible with a single gravitating dark matter fluid (which requires $w \simeq 0$), and instead arises from the collective interplay of cold dark matter and a phantom background field.

A realistic, dark-matter-dominated galactic halo in the original parameterization requires a power-law metric with $\epsilon \simeq 1.08$ (where $\rho_{\mathrm{total}} \simeq \rho_{\mathrm{DM}}$ and $\rho_{\mathrm{ph}} \simeq 0$), rather than the special logarithmic limit $\epsilon = 3/2$ frequently adopted as "Perfect Fluid Dark Matter."

At the $\epsilon = 3/2$ limit, the phantom component exhibits negative energy density ($\rho_{\mathrm{ph}} = -\frac{\lambda}{16\pi r^3} < 0$) and strongly violates the Null Energy Condition ($\rho_{\mathrm{ph}} + p_{r,\mathrm{ph}} = -\frac{3\lambda}{16\pi r^3} < 0$), meaning extrapolations to extreme astrophysical regimes (like high-energy particle collisions or intense magnetic fields) without accounting for stability bounds risk being unphysical.
